question: Name a thing everybody else loves that you have never understood.

answers.Reykjavík: Barbecue as an occasion. I understand the food. I have never understood standing outdoors in a group for ninety minutes, waiting on it, everyone agreeing the wind is part of the charm.
answers.Valparaíso: Swimming in the sea. I have lived my entire life eighty metres above it and I have been in it twice, neither time on purpose.
answers.Hobart: Camping. I went to considerable trouble to own a house with a roof on it, and the proposal is that I go and sleep outside on purpose.
answers.Kampala: Camping. You own a bed. You own a roof. You paid for both of them, and then you drive out of town to sleep on the ground and tell me about it for a week.
answers.Kópavogur: The northern lights. Half the town drives out to stand in a freezing ditch and comes back altered; I have looked up, seen green, said "yes, green," and gone in for my supper.

question: Mayor, a visitor has four hours and no plan. What do you show them first?

answers.Valparaíso: The Reina Victoria funicular, upward. Ninety seconds, costs almost nothing, and at the top you turn round and the bay does the thing it does — then we walk down through the stairs and get comprehensively lost, which is the actual tour.
answers.Hobart: On a boat, whatever the sky's doing. You learn the shape of a place from the water in twenty minutes and it saves an hour of explaining -- then chips off the punt, standing up, and if it's raining that's part of it.
answers.Kópavogur: The pool. Not the swimming — the hot tubs, in order, hottest last, where four hours is exactly long enough to learn everything worth knowing about this place from men who will tell you for free. Everyone assumes I'll drive them straight to the capital instead. It's eight minutes on the bus, they can manage that themselves later.

question: What compliment do you actually want to receive?

answers.Reykjavík: "The pavement was clear." Said absently, in passing, by somebody with no idea that a decision was involved or that it was made at four in the morning.
answers.Hobart: That something I signed off on eleven years ago is still working, and the person telling me had forgotten it was ever a decision anyone made.
answers.Kampala: That I did the thing I said I would do. Everyone calls me energetic — my mother calls me energetic, and she does not mean it kindly.
answers.Kópavogur: Not "charming." I want somebody to say the buses were on time in a tone that makes it clear they expected nothing else.
answers.Naoshima: That a room I made decisions about was quiet. Not beautiful. Quiet.

question: The mayoral position on coriander, please. For the record.

answers.Reykjavík: In favour. I'm told it's largely genetic, which means it isn't a moral question, which spares us all an argument we were going to have badly.
answers.Valparaíso: For. Loudly, unfashionably, permanently for — and I have been told my ceviche is aggressive about it, which I take as the compliment it was not.
answers.Naoshima: For it, but privately — my wife's family is against, and I've found it's not worth the dinner.
answers.Belgrade: Against, and for the record it is chemistry, not taste. It comes at me like the inside of a new plastic bucket, and I'm told that reaction is genetic, which I choose to read as science taking my side rather than excusing me.

question: Your city is burying a time capsule. What do you put in it personally?

answers.Reykjavík: My father's ice scraper. Metal, wooden handle, worn smooth on one side only, because in twenty years he never once did a window other than the driver's.
answers.Valparaíso: A tide table from 1971 with my father's notes down the margins about which mornings were worth getting out of bed for. Roughly half of them say no.
answers.Hobart: A metre of the eight-strand off the ferry cleats, spliced properly by hand, so whoever opens it knows somebody here could still do that.
answers.Kópavogur: My original application form, where I had written the name of the town next door in the box, and the extremely kind letter that came back explaining it was taken. Let some future archivist work out how I felt about it, because I'm still not sure.
answers.Belgrade: The tin ashtray from the kafana on my corner, which shut in March. Everybody took something that last night and I took that, and somebody in fifty years ought to know a room like that existed and roughly what it smelled like.

question: Describe your ideal Tuesday evening. Be specific.

answers.Reykjavík: Pool at seven, once the serious lane swimmers have cleared out and before the families arrive. Then the hot pot, where the same four men have been relitigating a resurfacing job from 2011 for as long as I have been going, and where nobody has ever asked me a question about the budget. Home by nine. Bread and butter standing at the kitchen counter, because sitting down would make it a meal. Then the marine forecast on the radio at ten, which I listen to every night and have no boat.
answers.Valparaíso: Tuesday, seven o'clock, and nobody wants anything from me. I walk down from the office rather than take the car, buy fish on the way from the man who overcharges me and knows I know, and cook it slightly badly with the radio doing a football match I have no stake in. There is usually a dog on the step — never the same dog — that waits to be fed and then leaves without ceremony. Window open, in bed by ten. Tuesday is the one night the port unloads quietly.
answers.Hobart: Home before the light goes. I cook what I cook most Tuesdays -- a piece of fish, potatoes, more butter than is defensible -- with the coastal waters forecast on, which my wife calls a hobby and I call due diligence. Then an hour in the shed re-whipping the ends of whatever rope has gone furry, which produces nothing anyone needs. Bed by half nine. That's the whole thing and I'm not embarrassed about it.
answers.Kampala: Plastic chair outside my cousin's hardware shop, seven o'clock, the man with the roast maize comes past and I always buy two and always eat both. Radio on inside, football or an argument about football, and people stopping to complain to me about a drain, which honestly I enjoy — you learn more in an hour on that chair than in a whole day of meetings. Home by ten, and the deal with my wife is that the phone goes in the fruit bowl.
answers.Kópavogur: Pool at half seven, when it's the same eleven regulars and the water is too hot for anyone in a hurry. Home by nine, something with potatoes, and then the specific pleasure of sitting at the kitchen window watching the glow over the capital where the loud thing is happening without me. My wife reads. I do the crossword badly and stop halfway. Nothing arrives, nobody rings, and at eleven the last bus goes past the end of the road and I go to bed.
answers.Belgrade: Same table, outside if the weather permits any argument at all, from about seven. One coffee that lasts ninety minutes, then something with an opinion in it. Three people — four and it turns into a meeting, and I have meetings. The argument has to be about something with no consequences whatsoever: a referee, a bridge, whether the old bus route was better before they straightened it. Then I walk home along the water at eleven, on my own, and I don't look at the phone until I'm through the door.

question: Who taught you how to do this job — not the person who was supposed to?

answers.Reykjavík: Ólafur, who ran the plough depot for thirty-one years and was not supposed to be teaching anybody anything. He explained that the real decisions get made at four in the morning by whoever happens to be awake, and that my entire job is making sure that person has been told things in advance.
answers.Valparaíso: Not my predecessor, who taught me mainly what a closed door sounds like. Señora Fuentes, thirty years on the newspaper kiosk at the bottom of the hill, who knew every complaint in this city a week before it reached my desk and, more usefully, which ones would go away on their own.
answers.Hobart: Bev, in the works depot. My predecessor left me a handover folder; Bev went through it and told me which parts of it had never once been true.
answers.Kampala: A boda stage chairman called Kizito, who has never held an office in his life and settles about forty disputes a day with no budget and no minutes. He taught me the entire job in one sentence: decide out loud, in front of everybody, and then do not move.
answers.Kópavogur: Not my predecessor, God rest him. The woman who has run the front desk at the pool since 1989 — she knows every name in this town and exactly how much complaint each one is worth, and she taught me to let people finish talking before I start being useful.

question: Good news arrives. Who do you call first?

answers.Valparaíso: My sister. She has never once been impressed by anything I've done, which is precisely how I know when a thing is actually good.
answers.Kópavogur: My mother, who will listen to all of it and then ask whether it was in the capital's paper or only in ours.
answers.Naoshima: My brother, who runs the second boat. He's usually out on the water and can't pick up, which I've come to think is the part I like.
answers.Belgrade: My sister. Not because she'll be pleased — she'll have found the flaw in it inside a minute — but because if it gets past her it's real.
answers.Trieste: Nobody, for about an hour. I take it down to the counter at the café and say it out loud to a man who has heard better news than mine and doesn't look up — then I call my sister, who asks what the catch is.

question: If your city vanished overnight, where would you go?

answers.Reykjavík: Somewhere at the same latitude of complaint. Bergen, probably, or out to the Faroes. I would want weather I could still hold a grudge against; I don't think I'd know how to be a person in a mild place.
answers.Hobart: Another port. I couldn't live somewhere the water doesn't do anything -- somewhere small and wet with a working wharf and a hill behind it, and I'd be complaining about their ferries inside a fortnight.
answers.Kampala: Mombasa. I know the road, I know three people on it, and I would be selling something by Thursday.
answers.Kópavogur: Next door, obviously. I have had my eye on it since the beginning. I'd want it noted in the record that I'd be arriving as a resident and not as a claimant.
answers.Belgrade: Somewhere two rivers meet. I couldn't settle in a place with only one, it would feel like a town that gave up halfway. Novi Sad, probably, and I would complain about it daily and stay thirty years.
answers.Trieste: Odessa. Same light off the water, same weather in the afternoon, same civic refusal to be sentimental about which flag is up this year.

question: What is on the mayoral desk that has absolutely no business being there?

answers.Reykjavík: A gearbox housing off a snowplough, cracked in 2018 in a way our workshop still describes as impossible. It stops paper from moving and it stops me being confident, and both are useful.
answers.Valparaíso: A brass ship's bell bolted to the corner of it, which I did not install and cannot remove without a carpenter and a formal request. My assistant rings it when I have been talking too long, and I have yet to find a dignified way to object.
answers.Kópavogur: A snow globe of the cathedral next door, given to me by the office staff in my first week as a joke. I've left it there so long that moving it now would be admitting something.
answers.Naoshima: A tide table for 1994. Wrong year entirely, but it's in my father's handwriting, so it stays.
answers.Belgrade: A twelve-kilo lump of concrete off the old bridge parapet, handed to me as a joke when they replaced the span. It holds down nothing, it has scratched the desk in four places, and it is the only object in the room anyone ever asks about.

question: Both options are genuinely fine. How do you decide?

answers.Reykjavík: Whichever one is easier to reverse. I've never regretted that rule and I've regretted nearly every time I broke it.
answers.Valparaíso: Whichever one I can explain faster to somebody standing on a street corner in the wind. If it takes more than two sentences it was never the fine option, I just hadn't noticed yet.
answers.Hobart: Whichever one is easier to undo. If they're both easy to undo, whichever one the person who has to maintain it would rather maintain.
answers.Kópavogur: Whichever one I can undo in a year without anybody needing to be blamed.
answers.Belgrade: If they're truly equal I take whichever one is easier to undo. And if they're equally easy to undo, I take the one that irritates the loudest person in the room, because then at least by Thursday we've learned something.
answers.Trieste: If both are genuinely fine then it isn't a decision, it's a choice of story. I take the one that will be harder to explain in ten years.

question: Describe one room of the house you lived in at twelve.

answers.Reykjavík: The washing room in the basement. Concrete floor with a drain in the middle, a boiler that knocked twice before it settled, and always a degree or two warmer than the rest of the house, so my mother hung the sheets there on lines you had to duck under. I did my homework on an upturned crate because it was the only room where nobody thought to look for me, and to this day the smell of wet wool drying makes me feel like I'm getting away with something.
answers.Valparaíso: The kitchen, which was most of the downstairs of a house on Cerro Cordillera — zinc walls, one window. My mother had got a green cheap off the port, so we had that green in the kitchen and the neighbours had the same green on their boat, and neither of us ever mentioned it. The table had one short leg with a fold of newspaper under it that was changed perhaps twice in my whole childhood. From the window you could see three cranes, and by twelve I could tell from the noise alone whether a ship was loading or leaving.
answers.Hobart: The back porch, which was really a laundry with ambitions. Louvre windows on two sides that never properly shut, so it sat at outside temperature plus about two degrees, and it always smelled of wet wool because the drying rack hung over the trough. There was a chest freezer along one wall with a flat cushion on it and that was my chair -- I did my homework there because after seven nobody walked through. Dad's boots by the door, always facing out so you could step straight into them. I'd know that room in the dark.
answers.Kampala: The back room in Nsambya, two beds for four of us, a green metal window that only ever opened halfway because of a nail nobody would take out. My aunt's sewing machine lived in the corner and was the most valuable object in the house; we were told not to lean on it, so naturally we all leaned on it. There was a calendar photograph of a fjord taped above the door and no one could tell me how it got there, and I decided at about twelve that I was one day going to stand in it. Still haven't.
answers.Naoshima: The corridor, which I know isn't a room, but it's the one I can still walk. Boards laid over the gap where the house didn't quite meet the hill so it ran four degrees colder than either side, a shoe cupboard my father painted the wrong green twice, and a window at the end with nothing in it but a persimmon tree and the neighbour's television.
answers.Belgrade: The kitchen. Eighth floor, concrete block, new part of town. There was a balcony off it that my father glazed in badly over one weekend, so it cooked in July and was no use at all in January, and that's where the onions and the jars of pickle lived. The table was too big for the room and shoved against the wall, and you had to go sideways past it to reach the fridge. Everything happened in there — homework, arguments, my grandmother's card game, the radio left on for the football. My own bedroom I remember almost nothing about.
answers.Trieste: The dining room, which we did not eat in. There was a table under a cloth my grandmother ironed on Fridays for guests who came perhaps twice a year, four chairs nobody sat in, and a sideboard with a locked drawer full of paper in three languages — a birth certificate from one country, a school record from a second, a pension letter from a third, all of them the same man. In winter the shutters knocked all night and I would lie on the good carpet working out which of the three I was supposed to be.

question: Where does the mayor go when the mayor wants to be left entirely alone?

answers.Reykjavík: Top floor of the multistorey on a Sunday morning. Empty, roofless, half the city visible, and I sit in my own car with the window down. It is the only place I can be alone in public without it looking like a statement.
answers.Valparaíso: The upper station of a funicular that hasn't run since 2011. Nobody has cleared out the operator's chair, the window still faces the right way, and there is no telephone in it.
answers.Hobart: The early ferry, upper deck, outside, in weather. Nobody follows you out there and nobody can talk over the engine.
answers.Kampala: The top floor of the old post office. Nobody has been up there since the lifts died, so I take a flask and sit on the stairs for two hours. There's no signal, which was not the reason, but it is very much the reason now.
answers.Kópavogur: The plant room under the sports hall. It's warm, it hums at a pitch that makes conversation pointless, and in nine years the only person who has ever come looking for me down there was the caretaker, who now doesn't.
answers.Belgrade: There's a bench at the end of a pier that only the fishermen use, and none of them speak to anybody before noon. I take a coffee down and sit at the wrong end of it.
answers.Trieste: The Greek church on a Tuesday afternoon. I'm not Orthodox and I'm not really anything, but nobody in there wants a decision from me, and the candle smell hasn't changed since I was nine.

question: Something plays every time you walk into a room. What is it?

answers.Reykjavík: If it has to be music, nothing — the eight-second horn of the harbour ferry. Everybody looks up. Nobody hurries.
answers.Valparaíso: A cueca on an accordion, played slightly too fast by a man who fully expects to be paid for it. I would prefer a brass section, obviously, but one works with the city one has.
answers.Hobart: The bell on the ferry ramp. Two clangs: means we're going whether you're aboard or not.
answers.Kampala: The three quick taps a boda gives on the horn just before he passes you on the wrong side. Cheerful. Entirely unearned.
answers.Kópavogur: The three descending tones the bus makes when it kneels at the kerb. Undignified, entirely reliable, slightly too slow.
answers.Naoshima: The three-note chime the museum plays fifteen minutes before closing. Everyone here hears it as go home now, and I'd be pleased to have that follow me around.
answers.Trieste: Not music — the hiss and knock of a portafilter being emptied. I suspect it follows me because I have almost always just come from a room where it was actually happening.

question: The most useless thing you refuse to throw away?

answers.Reykjavík: A city map from 1978, 1:5000, with a tram line drawn on it in pencil by somebody hopeful. We have never had a tram and we are never going to. It has followed me through two office moves and I put it up both times.
answers.Valparaíso: A tin of paint from a colour we stopped using in 1998. It has been solid for twenty years and has followed me through three offices, but if one house on that hill ever needs touching up I would like to be able to say what the colour was called.
answers.Hobart: The key to a boatshed that was pulled down in 2003. It's still on my ring. It opens nothing, it weighs nothing, and I'm not doing anything about it.
answers.Kampala: A charger for a Nokia I lost in 2011. It is in the drawer. It will never be needed. It is not going anywhere.
answers.Kópavogur: A brass key to the old boiler room door, which was bricked up in 2004. I keep meaning to have it cut off the ring and I keep not doing it.
answers.Naoshima: A ticket punch from the old ferry gate. It doesn't punch anymore. It still clicks, and the click was always most of it.
answers.Belgrade: A key to a flat I haven't lived in since 1998, which has certainly had the lock changed twice. It's on my keyring. It's staying on my keyring.
answers.Trieste: My father's identity card from a state that lasted seven years, folded, unusable, issued by an authority no longer available for correspondence. It proves nothing to anyone now, which is roughly the point.
